May there be no obstacle;
having bowed to the supreme Lord of Death, I shall hereafter proclaim the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*); listen with concentrated minds.
Then, for the sake of liberation from the bondage of karma known as the impurity of the self and illusion (māyā),
and for the manifestation of the state of Śiva, the knowledge of Śiva proceeds.
Knowledge is declared to be twofold: the higher and the lower.
The higher is called direct realization, while the lower is the supreme scripture.
At the time of creation, Maheśāna, for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human existence,
manifested pure knowledge characterized by five streams.
It is for the sake of attaining knowledge, a medicine whose nature is to gather [the teachings],
which is sweet with the happiness of its ultimate transformation, and which reveals its specific qualities.
In some cases, according to the Dharma, the effect [is perceived] through the cause;
in other cases, the cause [is perceived] through the effect, as seen in traditional scripture.
He is established as the Lord (pati) because he is the impeller of insentient things such as Māyā;
therefore, he is declared to be the knower of all objects.
In the Mataṅga, it is stated that for one whose prior gift consists of that [which is to be given], the procedure of the gift (*dānakriyā*) [is as follows].
Wear the supreme foundation, which consists of the rays of your own power;
you are the self, unwavering yet possessing a mobile form.
That very one is the ultimate limit, supremely subtle, consisting of the nectar of all directions;
she is the earth, peaceful, and intensely longing for the mere essence of reality.
The beginning and the end are metaphorically designated as having form;
in this world, they are perceived by consciousness as stable and mutually related.
Because his body exists, he performs the action;
in each respective instance, he acts through that very body which serves as the agent.
In the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"The instrument is neither a void power nor is it insentient consciousness;
because there would be no restriction regarding objects, it is one [in both] cognition and action. Thus it is.

Just as time, though formless, is seen to be the accomplisher of results, so too the agent is held to be threefold: the capable, the intent, and the engaged. The distinction among these is merely figurative, arising from the different modes of the capacity’s engagement.
The sign (*nimitta*) which is perceived as the auxiliary cause,
and that subtle material cause (*upādāna*) which is inherent in every effect— these two are the primary factors.
These [beings] are embodied, possessed of parts, and thus characterized by various forms and dimensions;
among them, the former [gross elements] consist of gross parts.
Therefore, there exists a certain intelligent Lord,
eternally established, who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and who is free from all objective states.
The fruit of the agent's action is to be known as belonging to this [consciousness];
even while sleeping, it remains awakening those who are capable of being awakened.
Obstructing those who are to be obstructed and ripening the karma of the agent,
making them fit for the manifestation of the power of *māyā*,
and seeing all that has been born...
The individual soul (paśu) is distinct from one another, limited by the body, pervasive [in its own sphere], differentiated, impure, insentient,
the enjoyer of the fruits of its own actions, the agent, possessing limited knowledge, and lacking sovereignty.
Now, the beginningless impurity (anādimala) of persons is proclaimed as their state of bondage (paśutva);
it should be understood as being like the husk or the outer shell of a grain, in relation to that which is the sprout of the seed of Māyā.
It is like the collection of powers belonging to one's own time and limit, which abide within each individual self.
Among them, the power of Maheśvara is Śivā, who bestows grace upon all;
When it assumes its unfolding at the end of the obstruction through the brilliance of its own intensity,
accompanied by transformation, then it is called the "object of grace" (anugrāhyakā).
Just as the Kuṇḍalinī power follows after Māyā and Karma,
so too does the world's existence consist of the resonance (*nāda*) arising from her.
p.
4) Of that [Speech], there are four modes (*vṛtti*) consisting of speech, namely *vaikhārī* and so forth:
*vaikhārī*, *madhyamā*, *paśyantī*, and the one known as *sūkṣmā*.
The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe— * * * * * * * * — the one, partless, subtle, beginningless, imperishable Lord.
That one [Principle] resides within the seed of inauspiciousness, possesses the manifold powers of the universe,
is the limit of the authority of auxiliary causes, is all-pervasive, and is imperishable.
In the pure [state], you are the infinite Lord established in the resonance;
the knots, the arts born thereof, time, knowledge, passion, and the subtle elements are yours.
From the gunas arise pride, anxiety, and patience respectively;
and action, consisting of both dharma and adharma, is likewise threefold.
Karma is called "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) because it is produced by activity and exists in a subtle state.
The realm of Janakaṇḍāraka is to be enjoyed; it is the means for the three [stages] beginning with the path-self, and because it is the source of both truth and untruth, it is the form [of reality].
During the cosmic sleep, [the world] undergoes maturation; its creator makes use of it.
At the end, he abides within Māyā; for that which has not been experienced does not perish.
Now, the self is pure, bound and yet again liberated,
insentient, all-pervading, eternal, devoid of qualities, and inactive.
Since consciousness, consisting of vision and action, exists at all times and in every respect within the Self,
it is heard that in liberation it is "all-pervading" (sarvatomanas).
In the absence of a bond, one must speak of dependence on another; for what is it that binds? If it were inherent, then the word "liberated" would be nullified.
He has arisen as the destroyer of the beginningless impurity; because he is free from beginningless impurity, he is the omniscient Śiva who pervades all.
When its having a beginning is established, then a cause is postulated;
by those two [beginning and cause], the pure and the impure are understood according to their true nature.
Just as the sign (nimitta) exists there, it does not exist in that same way for Śiva and the Self.
This [world], extending from the agent to the edge of the earth, which serves to accomplish the purpose of the rod of punishment,
is determined to be restricted to each individual soul, even though it is common to all.

Because it does not express [everything] simultaneously from all sides and because it does not arise [as a single whole], it does not encompass everything; yet, even though its constituent parts belong to different classes, they produce a single result, like the various components of a lamp.
For the sake of liberation, that bound soul is not [liberated] by anything else as long as attachment to the body has not ceased and it does not experience its enjoyments.
Into this aforementioned [Self], which is absolutely impure and immutable,
the *kalā* enters into union through the will of Śiva.
(6) Even though Maheśvara is all-pervading, his conjunction with a body occurs through *karman*;
because he lacks [such] power inherently, there is no lack of capacity on his part regarding the application of *karman*.
Because the power of consciousness in the bound soul (paśu) is obstructed by its state as a beast, its autonomy is [impaired];
therefore, being devoid of the capacity for action, it requires a director.
Because the Great Lord, the Uniter, [bestows it] by His own will with great power,
Vaikharī is the object of the ear, while Madhyamā is indeed characterized by conceptualization.
Or rather, the final cause of these [sounds] is the Void (*nirvī*);
by means of the functions of sound, the entire world is instantly awakened.
For there is never any cognition for a person apart from words;
indeed, this entire universe here follows after words.
In the ultimate sense, these very [powers] constitute the supreme bond for bound souls;
their consciousness is intensified by *kalā*, and their objective domain is revealed by *vidyā*.
And even when colored by passion, he is engaged in the functions of the intellect and other faculties;
having placed [the self] upon the path of the elemental self, from Māyā down to the earth.
The person, whose sole delight is in enjoyment, experiences the objects of enjoyment present there;
for this person, enjoyment consists of sensation characterized by pleasure and pain.
A person approaches that [body] through karma;
and from karma arise the objects and the instruments from the body.
For the sake of attaining enjoyments, they come into being and cease to be for the enjoyer;
likewise, the subtle individual soul (*jīva*), situated within the realm of Māyā, is [subject to this] due to its own intense defects.
He is the transmigrating being, the subject of objects, the enjoyer, the field, and indeed the knower of the field.
The embodied soul, being of the nature of bondage, is called "sakala" (the conditioned) by the wise;
this occurs when it is not yet freed from the power of tamas. Upon its liberation from that [power], [it becomes niṣkala].
Śiva manifests the infinity of vision and action for those embodied beings whose power falls away so as not to return, even though they are otherwise dear to the world.
For those whose worldly existence has ceased, their longing for liberation is the very sign of that state.
Because of the descent of that [desire], even in such an ignorant person,
why does a discerning intellect not arise, directed toward the Self?
In the discerning person, [discrimination] arises;
it is this that delivers the conscious being, endowed with the desire to know, from the ocean of transmigratory existence.
The Lord, the Impeller, joins this [soul] which was unjoined through the desire to impel;
the glorious King of Mantras is the impeller in the act of impelling.
In the discipline of the one to be favored and likewise in that of the one who favors,
because of compassion toward these two, their union is very difficult to obtain.
Having approached the Guide and being purified by initiation,
he becomes free from impurity and free from affliction, and attains union with Śiva.
In the Sarvajñānottara (p.
"One should not [perform] the initiation for those who are to be avoided..."
The agentive power of the individual soul (aṇu) is eternal, like the power of the Lord; though obscured by tamas, it shines forth through the grace of the Supreme.
He is called "all-knowing" because he knows the nature of consciousness and form;
yet he is said to be "knowing only a little" because of his perception of obstructions and the like.
Then the living being becomes conscious when it is joined with power;
otherwise, the self is indeed observed to be partless and devoid of consciousness.
Just as a teacher awakens his sleeping disciples before him,
so too Śiva awakens Śakti, who is asleep in the sleep of delusion.
Just as the power of those who are powerless arises from the efficacy of medicine, so too,
through the application of that potency, immeasurable capability comes to be.
The state of being Śiva is appropriate for liberation; the state of being a bound soul (paśu) is appropriate for the body.
And because his self is presided over by Īśvara, he is always independent;
thus, although he is a treasure-house of eternal, pervasive, and infinite power, the accomplishment of his goals is nonetheless established through external means.
The single knowledge of the manifold universe is of the nature of Śiva.
Pervasive, stainless, and peaceful, it is indeed a single reality characterized by the triad of enjoyment and liberation; its manifestation is supreme and immaculate.
Just as heat is inseparable from fire, O Lord, so too is the union of the Self and Śiva inseparable from Śambhu;
it is the supreme and non-supreme realization of Śiva.
Neither perceptual nor inferential,
that stainless knowledge always shines clearly regarding all objects.
From this extensive bondage, which obstructs the state beyond,
initiation alone liberates one upward and leads one even to the abode of Śiva.
That which is called "giving" is one's own very being, which consists of the nature of knowledge and action.
That power of his, through contact with the manifested elements, becomes pure;
it is manifested in the bound soul (paśu) by the grace of the Lord.
When one perceives the bodiless Self with the eye of knowledge,
then one becomes tranquil in soul, free from longing for everything.
The fire of initiation [consumes] the impurity of the living being; through the union with the [divine] lineage, one attains that which is well-proclaimed.
The region of the heart kissed by the power of the All-pervasive Lord, through the yoga of manifold stages, has attained supreme isolation.
Because it is devoid of beginningless impurity, one does not attain another state of existence—
that person for whom all phenomena dissolve in the waking state just as they do in deep sleep.
The thread of consciousness, suspended from that [Supreme], is sufficient for him;
the self, having reached its true state and being free from ritual observances, beholds Śiva together with Śakti and the other [principles].
Just as someone holding a torch in his hand might abandon the object he has been searching for once it is seen.
Having illuminated the object of knowledge through wisdom, one should abandon [the means];
when the mind, having attained its mark, dissolves into the supreme reality.
For at that time, all-encompassing consciousness undergoes destruction within that which is inexpressible,
without support, ungraspable, and devoid of mental activity.
The firm conclusion of the scripture is that he is liberated,
having been led from the states arising from worldly existence to a state that is unwavering and long-enduring.
Since he is liberated, his nature as Śiva is manifest, and he has accomplished all that was to be done,
there is no worship, no prostration, and no [recitation of] mantras here.
It is said that the object of knowledge is "only"; nothing at all is to be known.
Just as the wind, however swift it may be, does not go anywhere except through space.
But one whose mind is fixed upon the object of knowledge does not let go even while remaining amidst sense objects;
likewise, regarding that formless state which transcends the senses,
[the mind remains there] for as long as it takes to milk a cow, or the flight of an arrow, or even the mere opening of an eye.
One who is intent on the supreme state beyond action shall not attain [worldly gain];
having transcended the state of a bound soul (paśu), he abides in the state of the Lord (pati).
For him, what is called "going" is actually going everywhere;
for one who has immersed himself in the abode of Śiva and is an enjoyer of experience, there is never any [notion of] going at all.
The state of being an enjoyer is the imitation of [past] actions;
just as the power connected with poison is suppressed by mantras.
Just as that poison is not exhausted, so too [is the karma] of a person;
yet karma consisting of manifold states is burnt away like a seed.
Just as when the production of a jar has been completed, the wheel continues to spin even though its purpose is fulfilled;
This is known as that which is fully accomplished through past impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*);
it is like a lamp [remaining] when a jar has been broken.
O fair-faced one, when the body falls away, the Self likewise remains forever;
reveal this knowledge to my devotees.
Just as wealth must be protected from thieves.
Thus [ends the section].

This was written by Naṭarāja after seeing this palm-leaf manuscript, adorned with grantha script, from the Aḍaiyāra library; and this [work] is the Daśakārya, which provides instruction on the subject matter of the Āgamas.
It is seen written in the middle of the manuscript, and here at the very beginning of this work, it appears as follows (p.

Thus [ends the previous section]. From this point onward, beginning with the words "ityataḥ param," this manuscript is visible, though the concluding statement indicating the end is lost. Immediately following, there exists a text titled *Sītācakra* and *Rāmacakra*, written by this very same author. Furthermore, based on the identity of the handwriting, this too was written by the Śivācārya named Mahāgaṇapati.
It can be determined that it was written.
Thus spoke that King of Dancers.
